docs.title: Advanced Log Parser
docs.text: Article last updated: 2026-09-16.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Advanced Log Parser monitors log files from Pandora FMS. On each run it scans a directory, selects files by name and lines by content with regular expressions, and prints the matching lines as Pandora FMS log_module entries on standard output.

The plugin reads each log file incrementally. It keeps an index per log file and per source type, so a run captures only the lines written since the previous run instead of the whole file. Captured lines are encoded in Base64, which keeps the generated XML valid whatever the contents of the log.

The plugin runs as a Pandora FMS agent plugin (module_plugin), and it can also be run by hand. It creates no agent of its own: the log modules it emits belong to the agent that executes it.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: Systems where it has been tested Rocky 9; Windows 11 with the Pandora FMS agent for Windows Systems where it works Any Linux system supported by Pandora FMS

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Read access to the scanned directory and to the log files inside it.
  • Read and write access to the index directory. By default the plugin uses the temporary directory of the operating system: /tmp on most Linux systems, or the path in TMPDIR when that variable is set.
  • The user that runs the plugin must have those permissions, because the agent runs the plugin as its own user.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The plugin is distributed as a single binary. Two deployment paths are available.

Manual upload — copy the binary to the plugins directory of the Pandora FMS agent and make it executable. On Linux the plugins directory of the agent is /etc/pandora/plugins, and on Windows it is %ProgramFiles%\pandora_agent\util.

Collections — deploy the same binary to many agents at once from the Pandora FMS console. This route requires:

  • Remote configuration enabled on the agent, which is only available with the Tentacle transfer mode.
  • The unzip command on the agent. Each collection is transferred as a ZIP file and the agent extracts it locally.

Create the collection in Configuration → Collections, add the binary to it, and assign the collection to each agent from the Collection tab of the agent. The agent extracts the collection under a directory named after the collection short name, so the binary does not end up in the plugins directory:

Platform Path of the binary in the agent Linux /etc/pandora/collections/<short-name>/pandora_logparser Windows %ProgramFiles%\pandora_agent\collections\<short-name>\pandora_logparser.exe

On Linux /etc/pandora/collections is the same directory as /usr/share/pandora_agent/collections.

Because the path carries the short name, the module_plugin line must use the full path:

module_plugin /etc/pandora/collections/<short-name>/pandora_logparser --dir /var/log/myapp --name-regex '.+\.log' --idx-dir /var/tmp/pandora-logparser

The console keeps each collection in sync with an MD5 hash: when the collection changes in the console, the agent replaces its copy and discards any local modification. With remote configuration enabled the agent also overwrites its local pandora_agent.conf with the configuration stored in the console, so register the module from the console rather than editing the file on the agent.

docs.title: Register the plugin in the agent
docs.text:
Add a module_plugin block to the agent configuration file. The agent runs the plugin at its own interval and attaches the emitted log modules to itself:

module_begin
module_plugin /etc/pandora/plugins/pandora_logparser --dir /var/log/myapp --name-regex '.+\.log' --content-regex '(?i)error|critical' --source-type app_errors --idx-dir /var/tmp/pandora-logparser
module_end

The block needs no module_name: the plugin generates its own modules and the agent appends them unchanged, so a name there would not name anything you see in the console. The agent only uses it in its own log messages, and derives one when the directive is absent.

The first execution produces no data: the plugin records each matching file at its current end. Later executions capture only the new matching lines.

Always quote options that contain *, ?, | or other shell metacharacters, for example '.+\.log' or '(?i)error', so that the shell does not expand them. That is Linux shell quoting; the Windows agent runs the command through cmd.exe, where the rules are different. See Windows: non-ASCII values and shell metacharacters.

docs.title: Indexes and the source type
docs.text:
Each log file has one index per source type. The --source-type value is part of the identity of that index, which has three consequences:

  • Two modules that read the same log file must use different --source-type values. If they share it, they share the index and only the module that runs first sees the new lines.
  • Changing the --source-type of an existing module makes that module start again at the end of the file. Everything written since the last run of the previous source type is skipped.
  • The source field of the generated log modules carries the --source-type value verbatim, so it also identifies the data origin in Pandora FMS.

Do not reuse a --source-type value for a different log file and filter combination unless you intend to share the read position.

docs.title: Several modules over the same files
docs.text:
Define one module_plugin block per filter and give each block its own --source-type:

# Module for errors
module_begin
module_plugin /etc/pandora/plugins/pandora_logparser --dir /var/log/myapp --name-regex '.+\.log' --content-regex '(?i)error' --source-type app_errors --idx-dir /var/tmp/pandora-logparser
module_end

# Module for warnings
module_begin
module_plugin /etc/pandora/plugins/pandora_logparser --dir /var/log/myapp --name-regex '.+\.log' --content-regex '(?i)warn' --source-type app_warnings --idx-dir /var/tmp/pandora-logparser
module_end

docs.title: Configuration file
docs.text:
Use --config <path> to read the options from a UTF-8 file instead of, or in addition to, the command line:

dir = /var/log/myapp
name_regex = .+\.log
content_regex = (?i)error
source_type = app_errors
idx_dir = /var/tmp/pandora-logparser

File format:

  • One key = value per line. The valid keys are dir, name_regex, content_regex, content_regex_base64, source_type, idx_dir and max_line_bytes.
  • Whitespace around = is ignored and the value is trimmed. A pattern that must begin or end with a space uses the escape \x20.
  • # starts a comment only at the beginning of a line, so a value may contain #. Blank lines are ignored.
  • A UTF-8 BOM and CR/LF line endings are accepted.
  • The file may be partial: a key that is not present keeps its built-in default.
  • An unknown key, a duplicate key, an empty value, or a line without = is an error, and the run stops. The key config is rejected because recursion is not supported.
  • The configuration file must not exceed 4 MiB.

Precedence:

  • An option set explicitly on the command line wins per key over the value in the configuration file. An explicit --name-regex '.*' is still an explicit choice.
  • The content filter is resolved as a group. When the command line provides --content-regex or --content-regex-base64, the content_regex and content_regex_base64 keys of the file are ignored entirely.
  • Two content filter sources inside the same layer are an error: two command-line options, or both content_regex and content_regex_base64 in the file.
  • With no source at all, the default .* applies. At least one option source must provide dir.

docs.title: Windows: non-ASCII values and shell metacharacters
docs.text:
The plugin has no encoding problem of its own. On Windows, Go reads the command line through the wide-character API and converts it to UTF-8, and the plugin reads log files and configuration files as UTF-8. The corruption happens before the plugin starts.

The Windows agent runs every module_plugin as cmd.exe /c "<command>" and converts the command line from UTF-8 to the ANSI code page of the system. Non-ASCII text does not survive that conversion, so the plugin never receives the text you wrote.

The two failure modes are not equally visible:

Value Symptom dir The path does not exist after the conversion. The run fails with exit status 1. content_regex, name_regex The pattern compiles and never matches. The run succeeds, prints nothing and captures no data.

The second case is the dangerous one: nothing fails, so a non-ASCII pattern looks correct in the configuration while it quietly captures nothing.

docs.title: Metacharacters of cmd.exe
docs.text:
The command also passes through cmd.exe, so its metacharacters stay active. Single quotes are not quoting characters for cmd.exe, so they never protect a pattern:

module_plugin ... --content-regex '(?i)error|critical' ...

'critical'' is not recognized as an internal or external command

Double quotes inside the pattern do protect it, because they survive the outer quotes the agent adds around the whole command. % is the exception, because cmd.exe expands it before the plugin starts:

Pattern contains Without quotes With double quotes | fails, exit status 255 works & fails, exit status 1 works < fails, exit status 1 works > fails silently, exit status 0 works ^ fails silently, exit status 0 works a lone % works works %NAME% fails silently fails silently

A silent failure is the dangerous case: the run reports success, the plugin receives a truncated pattern, and it then captures lines the pattern you wrote would never match. ^ is the sharpest example, because it is the anchor at the start of patterns such as ^ERROR: unprotected, the anchor disappears and the pattern matches anywhere in the line.

The two % rows are consistent: cmd.exe only expands a name between two percent signs, and double quotes do not prevent that expansion.

Only the configuration file and Base64 avoid every case above. Use one of them whenever a pattern contains any of these characters.

docs.title: Passing non-ASCII values
docs.text:
Only the first of these routes works for a path.

Configuration file (--config) — the only route for a non-ASCII dir. The command line carries only the path to the file, which must be ASCII, and the values inside the file are read as UTF-8 from disk, so they never travel through the code page conversion:

dir = C:\registros_日本語_Ошибка
content_regex = (?i)error|critical
source_type = app_errors

module_plugin "%ProgramFiles%\pandora_agent\util\pandora_logparser.exe" --config "C:\ProgramData\PandoraFMS\logparser.conf"

Base64 (--content-regex-base64) — for the content pattern. Base64 is ASCII and carries no shell metacharacter, so it avoids both the code page and cmd.exe. Generate the value from the UTF-8 bytes of the pattern:

printf '%s' 'Ошибка' | base64

That command prints 0J7RiNC40LHQutCw. On Windows, use PowerShell:

[Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes('Ошибка'))

Unicode escapes (\x{...}) — keeps the command line ASCII without a configuration file. The Go regular expression engine resolves them, so they are valid in --content-regex and --name-regex:

--content-regex '\x{041E}\x{0428}\x{0418}\x{0411}\x{041A}\x{0410}'

An escape works inside a regular expression only. There is no escape syntax for a path: \x{...} in --dir is the name of a literal directory.

docs.title: What does not work
docs.text:
• Non-ASCII text on the command line. The agent converts it before the plugin starts, so --dir fails with exit status 1 and --content-regex fails silently.
  • Writing the values in the ANSI code page inside pandora_agent.conf. The agent reads the command line as UTF-8 and converts it to ANSI, so ANSI bytes are already corrupted before that conversion.
  • Single quotes around a pattern that contains any of the metacharacters above. cmd.exe does not treat single quotes as quoting, so the pattern is split and the run fails.
  • A pattern containing %NAME%. cmd.exe expands it before the plugin starts and double quotes do not prevent it, so no command-line form works. Use the configuration file.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Confirm the plugin works before wiring it into the agent. The example uses a fresh directory.

  1. Create the log file and run the plugin once:
touch /var/log/myapp/app.log
pandora_logparser --dir /var/log/myapp --name-regex '.+\.log' --content-regex '(?i)error' --source-type app_errors --idx-dir /var/tmp/pandora-logparser

The first run prints nothing and exits with status 0: it has recorded the file at its current end.

  1. Append a matching line:
printf 'ERROR: disk full\n' >> /var/log/myapp/app.log
  1. Run the plugin again:
pandora_logparser --dir /var/log/myapp --name-regex '.+\.log' --content-regex '(?i)error' --source-type app_errors --idx-dir /var/tmp/pandora-logparser

It now prints one log_module entry:

<log_module>
  <source><![CDATA[app_errors]]></source>
  <data>"RVJST1I6IGRpc2sgZnVsbA=="</data>
  <encoding>base64</encoding>
</log_module>
  1. Decode the value of data to confirm the captured text:
printf 'RVJST1I6IGRpc2sgZnVsbA==' | base64 -d

ERROR: disk full

A third run with no new lines prints nothing and exits with status 0. Files with no new matching lines produce no entry, and a run in which nothing matches writes nothing to standard output at all.

docs.title: Incremental reading
docs.text:
The plugin keeps one index per log file and source type in --idx-dir. The index records the byte offset where reading stopped.

When the plugin encounters a log file for the first time it records the file at its current end and captures nothing, so historical content is never dumped. On later runs it reads from the recorded offset and processes only the new lines.

Removing or losing an index makes that log file start again at end-of-file: the next run records the file at its current end and skips the lines already written.

The scan is not recursive. Only the files directly inside --dir are considered, and subdirectories are ignored.

docs.title: Rotation and truncation
docs.text:
The plugin detects when a log file has been replaced or truncated:

  • If the file was renamed and a new file was created under the same name, the plugin detects the new file and reads it from the beginning.
  • If the file is smaller than the saved position, the plugin restarts the read from the beginning.

docs.title: Index maintenance
docs.text: On every run the plugin removes indexes whose log file no longer exists, which prevents the index directory from growing with entries for deleted logs. It never touches index files that it does not own.

docs.title: Matching model
docs.text:
• Matching is applied to each physical line of the log.
  • Matching is case-sensitive. A pattern that should ignore case needs an explicit (?i), as in (?i)error.
  • A multi-line entry such as a stack trace is captured as separate line fragments and cannot be matched as a whole.
  • The text is treated as UTF-8. UTF-16 and platform code pages are not decoded, so a UTF-8 pattern does not match a log file written in another encoding.
  • A leading UTF-8 BOM in a log file is removed before matching, so ^ anchors still apply to the first line.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
For every scanned file that has new matching lines, the plugin emits one log_module entry:

Field Content source The value of --source-type, verbatim. It identifies the data origin in Pandora FMS. data The matched lines joined by newlines and encoded in Base64, between double quotes. The XML serializer writes each quote as ". encoding Always base64.

The plugin creates no numeric or status module: log modules are its only output.

docs.title: Run the plugin manually
docs.text:
The plugin takes every option on the command line:

pandora_logparser --dir <path> [options]
pandora_logparser --config <path> [options]

Capture all new lines from .log files:

pandora_logparser --dir /var/log/myapp --name-regex '.+\.log' --idx-dir /var/tmp/pandora-logparser

Filter only the lines that match a pattern:

pandora_logparser --dir /var/log/myapp --name-regex '.+\.log' --content-regex '(?i)error' --source-type app_errors --idx-dir /var/tmp/pandora-logparser

Filter by file name and content with a custom index directory:

pandora_logparser --dir /opt/app/logs --name-regex 'access.*\.log' --content-regex '^50[023]' --source-type http_errors --idx-dir /var/tmp/pandora-logparser

Read every option from a configuration file:

pandora_logparser --config /etc/pandora/logparser.conf

docs.title: Diagnostics and exit status
docs.text:
The plugin has no verbose or debug option. Standard output carries only the generated XML, and every diagnostic goes to standard error, so redirecting the two streams separately keeps the data clean.

Warnings are issued when an index cannot be resolved or created, when an index cannot be loaded, when orphan cleanup fails, and when a line is skipped for exceeding --max-line-bytes. Errors are issued when a directory or a log file cannot be read, when a log module cannot be built, and when an index cannot be saved.

The exit status is 0 for a successful run or for --help, and 1 for invalid input or for a processing error.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A line longer than --max-line-bytes is skipped with a warning and the file keeps working. The default is 1048576 bytes.
  • A file that does not end with a newline keeps its trailing partial line unread until the terminator arrives. A line that is never terminated is never emitted.
  • The plugin validates at most the 64 KiB immediately before the saved offset. An in-place rewrite that leaves the file identity, the size and those bytes unchanged is not detected.
  • Only UTF-8 is decoded.
  • The plugin is not recursive and ignores subdirectories.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Check No output on the first run Expected behaviour: the index records each file at its end. Append a matching line and run the plugin again. A module never produces data Another module uses the same --source-type over the same file, or the source type was changed and the index restarted at end-of-file. Give each module its own --source-type; see Indexes and the source type. A pattern that worked elsewhere matches nothing Matching is case-sensitive, or the log file is not UTF-8. Add (?i) if case must be ignored; confirm the file encoding. A non-ASCII pattern matches nothing on Windows The agent converted the command line to the ANSI code page before the plugin started. Put the value in the configuration file, or use --content-regex-base64; see Windows: non-ASCII values and shell metacharacters. A module whose pattern has an alternation never runs on Windows cmd.exe splits the command at the bare pipe. Move the pattern to the configuration file or pass it in Base64. A line is missing from the output The line exceeds --max-line-bytes, or it was still unterminated when the plugin ran. Check the warning on standard error; raise --max-line-bytes if needed. error: --dir is required unless the config file provides dir Neither the command line nor the configuration file provides a directory. Pass --dir, or add dir to the configuration file. A very long pattern is rejected or truncated on Windows The Windows command line has a length limit and Base64 inflates the pattern. Put the pattern in the configuration file.

docs.title: Command-line options
docs.text: Name Required Default Description --dir <path> Yes, unless the configuration file provides dir — Directory to scan for log files. The scan is not recursive. --config <path> No — Read the parameters from a UTF-8 configuration file. --name-regex <regex> No .* Regular expression to filter file names. --content-regex <regex> No .* Regular expression to filter log lines. Conflicts with --content-regex-base64. --content-regex-base64 <value> No — Base64 value that decodes to the content regular expression. Conflicts with --content-regex. --source-type <name> No syslog Value of the source field of the generated log modules and part of the index identity. An empty value falls back to syslog. --idx-dir <dir> No Temporary directory of the operating system Directory where the index files are stored. It is created if it does not exist. --max-line-bytes <n> No 1048576 Maximum accepted log line size in bytes. Must be a positive integer. -h, --help No — Print the help and exit with status 0.

docs.title: Configuration file keys
docs.text:
Key Default Description dir — Directory to scan. Equivalent to --dir. name_regex .* Equivalent to --name-regex. content_regex .* Equivalent to --content-regex. content_regex_base64 — Equivalent to --content-regex-base64. source_type syslog Equivalent to --source-type. idx_dir Temporary directory of the operating system Equivalent to --idx-dir. max_line_bytes 1048576 Equivalent to --max-line-bytes. It must be a valid integer.

content_regex and content_regex_base64 cannot both be present in the same file.

docs.title: Regular expression syntax
docs.text:
Patterns accept the common regular expression constructions, including (?i) for case-insensitive matching, POSIX classes such as [[:digit:]], hexadecimal escapes such as \x20, and Unicode escapes such as \x{041E}. Lookaround is not supported: a pattern such as a(?=b) is rejected.

Examples for the file name filter:

.+\.log              → only files with the .log extension
access.*\.log        → files that start with "access" and end in ".log"
(app|sys)\.log       → files named "app.log" or "sys.log"

Examples for the content filter:

(?i)error                → lines containing "error", ignoring case
(?i)error|critical|fail  → lines containing error, critical or fail
^ERROR                   → lines that start with ERROR
[0-9]{3}\s               → lines with a three-digit code followed by a space

--content-regex-base64 accepts the standard and URL-safe Base64 alphabets, padded or unpadded, and must decode to valid UTF-8; a leading BOM and trailing CR/LF bytes are ignored. To pass non-ASCII values through the Windows agent, see Windows: non-ASCII values and shell metacharacters.

docs.title: Apache Enterprise Plugin
docs.text:
Article last updated: 2026-10-27.

Discovery integration recommended

For new installations use Apache Discovery, which is the recommended integration for this service. This plugin is the legacy path.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
The Apache Enterprise Plugin reads the mod_status page of an Apache HTTP Server and turns its counters into Pandora FMS modules: request and traffic rates, total accesses and traffic, CPU load, uptime, restart time, requests in progress, idle workers and an availability check.

The plugin runs as an agent plugin. The Pandora FMS software agent executes it, reads the module XML it prints on standard output and stores the values in the agent that runs it. Nothing is installed on the Apache server: the plugin only makes an HTTP request to a status URL that must already exist.

This page documents the server monitoring plugin. Discovering Apache servers and generating their agents is a different addon, documented in Apache Discovery.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: Scope State Evidence Addon Apache, version 1.0 Documented target The version this page describes. See Addon identity Pandora FMS NG 784 and later Supported The Marketplace states that all its integrations are compatible with these versions. This is a published compatibility statement covering the addon, not a test record for it curl on the host that runs the plugin Required The plugin retrieves the status page by running the curl command; it has no other HTTP client Network access from the Pandora FMS agent to the status URL Required Prerequisite, not a compatibility statement An Apache mod_status page served over HTTP Required The plugin parses the text of that page. See Enable the status page Basic-authentication credentials for the status location, when it is protected Required when the location requires authentication The plugin sends them with -user and -pass Apache HTTP Server versions Not validated No test record has been published for this addon. The legacy guide stated Apache 1.3 or later; nothing in the available evidence establishes that range Operating system of the host that runs the plugin Not validated No operating system has been recorded for this version. The legacy guide stated it was developed and tested on Rocky Linux and Fedora 34; no record confirms it Apache module set and MPM Not validated The available counters depend on the server configuration, not on the plugin

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Apache mod_status enabled and reachable from the Pandora FMS agent, with ExtendedStatus On so that the counters the plugin reads are present.
  2. A status URL that serves the HTML status page. The plugin extracts the counters from the text of that page, so a machine-readable variant such as server-status?auto does not provide the lines it looks for.
  3. curl available in PATH for the user that runs the Pandora FMS agent.
  4. Basic-authentication credentials, when the status location is protected.
  5. A Pandora FMS software agent on the host that runs the plugin, to execute it and ingest its modules.

The plugin only reads the status page. No official source identifies a narrower set of Apache permissions; restrict who can reach the status location, as it exposes request data.

docs.title: Enable the status page
docs.text:
Create the status location in a file included by the Apache configuration. The exact path depends on the distribution; on a Red Hat-family layout it is a file under /etc/httpd/conf.d/, for example /etc/httpd/conf.d/server-status.conf:

ExtendedStatus On

<Location "/server-status">
    SetHandler server-status
    Require valid-user

    AuthType Basic
    AuthName "Restricted Access"
    AuthUserFile /etc/httpd/.htpasswd
</Location>

Create the password file and the account the plugin will use, then reload or restart the service:

sudo htpasswd -c /etc/httpd/.htpasswd <USERNAME>

The status location is open to anyone who can reach it unless the configuration restricts it. The snippet above requires a user; Require ip <MONITORING_HOST_IP> restricts it by address instead, and both can be combined.

Check that the page loads before configuring the plugin:

curl -s -u <USERNAME>:<PASSWORD> 'http://<TARGET_HOST>/server-status'

The response must contain the human-readable counter lines (Total accesses:, requests/sec, idle workers, ...). A response with ExtendedStatus off, or a ?auto page, does not carry the lines the plugin reads.

docs.title: Install the plugin
docs.text:
Download the addon from the Pandora FMS Marketplace entry, which is limited to licensed users:

https://marketplace.pandorafms.com/entries/Apache

Copy the pandora_apache executable to the host that runs the Pandora FMS agent, for example into /etc/pandora/plugins/, and give it execute permission:

sudo chmod 755 /etc/pandora/plugins/pandora_apache

Nothing is installed on the Apache server, and no Apache client tools are needed on the monitoring host beyond curl.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
The plugin takes its configuration from two sources:

built-in defaults < configuration file < command-line options

The configuration file is optional. When it is used, it must be the first argument of the command line, and it is a plain-text file with one key=value pair per line. Command-line options override the file values.

docs.title: Agent configuration
docs.text:
Declare the plugin in the Pandora FMS agent configuration file, /etc/pandora/pandora_agent.conf, with a module_plugin line:

module_plugin /etc/pandora/plugins/pandora_apache -url http://<TARGET_HOST>/server-status -user <USERNAME> -pass <PASSWORD>

The agent executes the line on every execution cycle, reads the module XML the plugin prints and stores the modules in its agent. Use the absolute path of the executable, and keep the whole invocation on one line: the agent splits it on whitespace, so a password that contains spaces breaks the line.

If the installation uses centralized agent configuration, add the same module_plugin line there instead of editing the local file.

docs.title: Configuration file and options
docs.text:
A configuration file keeps the credentials out of the module_plugin line:

url=http://<TARGET_HOST>/server-status
user=<USERNAME>
pass=<PASSWORD>

The file is passed as the only positional argument:

./pandora_apache /etc/pandora/plugins/apache.conf

The same run with options only, without a file:

./pandora_apache -url 'http://<TARGET_HOST>/server-status' -user <USERNAME> -pass <PASSWORD>

Key points:

  • url is the complete status URL, including the scheme. It defaults to http://127.0.0.1/server-status, so a run that omits it queries the local server.
  • Options use the single-dash form with a separate value: -url <value>. The forms --url <value> and -url=<value> are read as different keys and have no effect, and a trailing option without a value is silently dropped.
  • Any option that the plugin does not use is accepted and ignored, so a misspelling does not stop the run — it silently leaves the documented value in place.
  • preffix (spelled with the double f) is prepended to every module name. Leave it empty for a single Apache instance per agent. To monitor two instances from the same agent, give each one a different prefix; otherwise the second run overwrites the modules of the first, because the names are identical.
  • The configuration file accepts # comment lines. Keys and values are trimmed and the last occurrence of a repeated key wins.

docs.title: Credentials and transport
docs.text:
• The plugin authenticates with HTTP Basic authentication only. It sends credentials when both user and pass are set; with only one of them the request goes out without authentication and the status page answers with an HTTP error.
  • The password is passed to curl as a command-line argument, so it is visible in the operating system process list while the request runs (ps, for example), and it is stored in clear text in the configuration file or in the module_plugin line.
  • Restrict the configuration file and the agent configuration to the user that runs the agent, for example chmod 600. There is no separate credentials file and no environment-variable input.
  • With an http URL the credentials and the status page travel unencrypted. With an https URL the traffic is encrypted, but the plugin accepts any server certificate: it does not validate it, so HTTPS gives confidentiality without authenticating the server.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Run the plugin manually from the host that runs the agent, with the configuration file or with the options:

./pandora_apache -url 'http://<TARGET_HOST>/server-status' -user <USERNAME> -pass <PASSWORD>

Each run executes once and exits. A successful run prints one XML <module> block per metric on standard output, in this form:

<module>
    <name><![CDATA[Apache Connection]]></name>
    <type>generic_proc</type>
    <data><![CDATA[1]]></data>
</module>
<module>
    <name><![CDATA[Apache requests/sec]]></name>
    <type>generic_data</type>
    <data><![CDATA[0.3400]]></data>
    <unit><![CDATA[rq/sec]]></unit>
</module>
<module>
    <name><![CDATA[Apache last restart]]></name>
    <type>generic_data_string</type>
    <data><![CDATA[Tuesday, 14-Oct-2025 08:12:34 CEST]]></data>
</module>

A module has a <description> element only when the status URL returned an HTTP status other than 200; in that case the description carries the HTTP error.

The exit status is 0 whenever modules are printed, including runs that could not reach the server, and 1 only when the command line is empty. Do not use the exit status to decide whether the request worked.

In the console, the agent that runs the plugin shows the modules on its next execution. Confirm that a numeric module such as Apache requests/sec receives values.

docs.title: Understand the results
docs.text:
The plugin generates the same eleven modules on every successful run. They cover four areas:

  • Availability. Apache Connection reports 1 when the status URL answered HTTP 200 and 0 for any other HTTP status code.
  • Throughput. Apache requests/sec, Apache KB/sec and Apache KB/request report the rates of the moment, in requests per second, kilobytes per second and kilobytes per request.
  • Totals since the last restart. Apache total accesses, Apache total traffic and Apache last restart describe the accumulated counters, which reset when the server restarts.
  • Load and workers. Apache CPU Load, Apache current requests and Apache iddle workers report the load figure, the requests being processed and the idle worker count.

Notes:

  • Most numeric modules are printed with four decimals (0.3400, 1234.0000), even for values that are integers on the status page. Apache CPU Load is the exception, described below.
  • Apache KB/sec and Apache KB/request are always in kilobytes: the plugin converts bytes by dividing by 1024 and megabytes by multiplying by 1024. Apache total traffic keeps the unit the status page reports (kB, MB, ...) as the module unit.
  • Apache server uptime is published in seconds, computed from the Server uptime line. A year counts as 360 days in that conversion.
  • Apache CPU Load reads the second field of the Server load: line when the page has one; that field can carry the percentage in parentheses, for example (5%), which is not a plain number. When the page has no such line, the plugin publishes the % CPU load figure with two decimals.
  • Apache iddle workers is the module name as the plugin publishes it, with that spelling. Use it verbatim when you define alerts or dashboards.
  • When preffix is set, it is prepended to every name above.
  • A counter that is missing from the status page (typically because ExtendedStatus is off) is published as a zero — 0.0000 in the modules with four decimals, 0.00 in Apache CPU Load — and a missing Restart Time line is published as an empty string. A zero does not necessarily mean the server reported zero.
  • Apache Connection is 1 when the response could not be interpreted at all, as well as on HTTP 200. See Operate and troubleshoot.

docs.title: Everyday operation
docs.text:
• The plugin keeps no state between runs: every execution reads the status page at that moment, so it can be run manually at any time without affecting the next scheduled run.
  • The Pandora FMS agent runs the plugin with the agent's own execution cycle. Use the agent configuration to change how often the counters are read.
  • The plugin sets no timeout on the request: a status location that accepts the connection and never answers keeps the run blocked until curl returns or the agent terminates it. The timeout key is read but not applied, and curl is invoked without a time limit.
  • There is no verbose or debug mode: -debug 1 is accepted but produces no additional diagnostics.
  • Use a different preffix per Apache instance when one agent runs the plugin against several servers.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Apache Connection is 1 but every counter reads zero — the request did not complete. A failure that stops curl (no curl in PATH, DNS failure, connection refused, TLS error) leaves the availability module at 1 and prints the rest of the modules with zeros, together with a Perl warning on standard error. Check that curl exists for the agent user and that the URL is reachable from the agent host; do not rely on Apache Connection alone to detect an unreachable server.
  • Apache Connection is 0 and the module description shows an HTTP error — the status location answered with that code. 401 means the credentials are missing or wrong: check user and pass. The plugin sends credentials only when both are set, so a run with just one of them also produces a 401. 403 is an access rule rejecting the agent address. 404 is a wrong path. A 301/302 means the URL redirects: the plugin does not follow redirects, so point it at the final URL.
  • The page loads in a browser but every counter reads zero — the URL is not serving the HTML status page the plugin parses (for example a ?auto endpoint), or ExtendedStatus is off so the counters are absent. Compare the URL with the one you tested in Enable the status page.
  • No module XML is printed — the command line was empty. The plugin then prints its usage summary on standard error and exits with status 1. There is no help option: -h is treated as an unknown key and the plugin runs against the default URL.
  • A run against the wrong server — url was omitted and the default http://127.0.0.1/server-status was used, or the option was written as --url/-url=... and ignored.
  • The configuration file seems to be ignored — it was not the first argument, or it cannot be opened. An unreadable file prints its error on standard error and the run continues with the built-in defaults instead of stopping, so the plugin may end up querying http://127.0.0.1/server-status. Check the argument order and the file permissions.
  • Two Apache servers overwrite each other's modules — both runs publish the same module names. Give each one a different preffix, or use one agent per server.
  • Alert thresholds fire on zeros after an Apache restart — the totals reset with the server. Compare Apache total accesses and Apache total traffic against the value of Apache last restart before treating a drop as an incident.

docs.title: Configuration keys
docs.text:
The same keys are accepted in the configuration file and as single-dash options.

Name Required Default Description url No http://127.0.0.1/server-status Complete URL of the HTML mod_status page, including the scheme. user Required when the status location is protected — User for HTTP Basic authentication. Applied only together with pass. pass Required when the status location is protected — Password for user. Applied only together with user. preffix No Empty Text prepended to every generated module name. Spelled with the double f.

Other keys are accepted and ignored, including timeout, tag and debug. In the configuration file, blank lines and lines starting with # are skipped, keys and values are trimmed, and the last occurrence of a repeated key wins.

docs.title: Command-line execution
docs.text:
./pandora_apache [config-file] [ -key value ... ]
Condition Behavior The command line is empty The plugin prints its usage summary on standard error and exits with status 1; no module is generated The first argument names an existing file The plugin reads it as the configuration file and applies the remaining options over its values The first argument does not name a file It is read as an option or ignored; the file is not loaded -key value Replaces the value of key from the file or the defaults --key value or -key=value Read as a different key and ignored, so the documented key keeps its default or file value A trailing option without a value Silently dropped; no error is reported An unknown key Accepted and ignored; the key set is not validated -h or --help No help option exists: it is treated as an unknown key Exit status 0 whenever modules are printed, including HTTP errors and unreachable servers; 1 only for an empty command line

docs.title: Generated modules
docs.text:
Modules are printed in this order, with preffix prepended to each name when it is set.

Module Type Value Unit Apache Connection generic_proc 1 when the status URL answered HTTP 200, 0 for any other HTTP status code — Apache CPU Load generic_data Load figure of the status page — Apache requests/sec generic_data Requests per second rq/sec Apache KB/sec generic_data Traffic per second, converted to kilobytes KB/sec Apache KB/request generic_data Traffic per request, converted to kilobytes KB/rq Apache last restart generic_data_string Value of the Restart Time line — Apache server uptime generic_data Uptime in seconds — Apache total accesses generic_data Accesses since the last restart — Apache total traffic generic_data Traffic since the last restart Unit reported by the status page Apache current requests generic_data Requests currently being processed — Apache iddle workers generic_data Idle workers —

docs.title: Addon identity
docs.text: Field Value Marketplace identifier Apache Marketplace name Apache Enterprise Plugin Addon version 1.0 Marketplace package Apache.1.0.64 Marketplace last update 2025-06-10 License One — download limited to licensed users Marketplace type Miscelaneus Workflow Monitoring plugin, agent plugin mode Executable pandora_apache

docs.title: Autodiscover
docs.text: Article last updated: 2026-10-05.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
The Autodiscover plugin finds the system services of an endpoint and turns them into Pandora FMS modules. It runs as an agent plugin: the agent executes it, the plugin prints the module definitions as XML on standard output, and the agent ingests them.

The plugin has two operating modes, and it needs one of them to do anything:

  • Built-in list (--default) — monitors a list of common services (databases, web servers, mail servers, containers...) that is built into the plugin. Each entry is matched against the whole service name, so ssh never selects sshd-keygen@rsa.
  • Custom list (--list) — monitors exactly the services you name, as substrings or regular expressions.

An endpoint has many units that are not running and does not have every service of the built-in list installed; the plugin reports only what matches the list it is given, so a run is not a report about the health of the whole endpoint.

  • Result. One generic_proc status module per service that exists in the service manager and matches the active list: 1 while the service is running and 0 while it is stopped or inactive. A name of the list that does not exist on the endpoint produces no module at all.
  • Optional usage. With --usage, the plugin also adds a CPU usage module and a memory usage module for each running service whose process can be resolved and whose usage is greater than zero.
  • Scope. The plugin reads the service manager of the endpoint: systemd on Linux, the service command and /etc/init.d when systemd is not available, and the Service Control Manager on Windows.
  • Coverage. Matching services are reported; nothing is discovered beyond the list you choose.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: Scope State Evidence Plugin version 2.1 Documented target The version this page describes Linux with systemd Tested Exercised on Fedora 44 (systemd 259) and Rocky Linux 10.2 (systemd 257): built-in list, custom lists, exclusions, verbose diagnostics and oneshot filtering Linux without systemd (SysV) Not validated No SysV-only host has been recorded Windows (Service Control Manager, amd64) Tested Exercised on Windows 11: built-in list, substring and exact matching, exclusions, .service suffix, three-character rule and --usage Windows service names shorter than three characters Required The plugin discards list entries under three characters on Windows, see Matching rules An agent able to run module_plugin entries on the endpoint Required Prerequisite, see Requirements

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. A Pandora FMS agent installed on the endpoint. The plugin is executed by the agent; it is not a server plugin and it does not need the Pandora FMS server.
  2. Linux: systemd, or the service command together with the /etc/init.d scripts when systemd is not booted. The plugin detects systemd at run time and falls back to SysV automatically.
  3. Windows: no additional component. The plugin reads the Service Control Manager.
  4. Permissions to query the services of the endpoint. Reading every service status and the resource usage of its process may require elevated privileges.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The plugin is distributed inside the agent package and needs no separate installation. The agent launches it through module_plugin, so no full path is required on Linux:

Platform Executable Linux /usr/share/pandora_agent/plugins/autodiscover Windows %PROGRAMFILES%\Pandora_Agent\util\autodiscover.exe

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
The whole configuration surface of the plugin is the agent configuration file: it has no configuration file of its own. Add one module_plugin entry per run you want, using the module_begin / module_end block to set a timeout.

The agent configuration shipped with the agent already contains this block:

# Service autodiscovery plugin
module_begin
module_plugin autodiscover --default
module_timeout 30
module_end

On Windows the same block names the executable explicitly:

# Service autodiscovery plugin
module_begin
module_plugin "%PROGRAMFILES%\Pandora_Agent\util\autodiscover.exe" --default
module_timeout 30
module_end

docs.title: Choose what to monitor
docs.text:
• Built-in list. Keep --default to monitor the services common to most servers. The list per platform is in Built-in default service list.
  • Custom list. Replace it with --list "<service1,service2>". Quote the value so the shell does not expand it, and separate the entries with commas.
# Monitor only the web server and SSH, by name
module_plugin autodiscover --list "httpd,sshd"

# Monitor the services matching a pattern
module_plugin autodiscover --list "apache.*,php[0-9.]*-fpm" --exact-match

docs.title: Narrow and refine the selection
docs.text:
• --exclude "<service1,service2>" removes services from the active list, whether it comes from --default or from --list. It is not an action of its own: it can be repeated, and the values accumulate. An entry that matches nothing is informational only.
  • --exact-match makes each --list entry match the whole service name instead of a substring. Use it when a name such as cron also selects cronie or crond. The built-in list always matches exactly.
  • --skip-oneshot (Linux with systemd only) ignores units whose type is oneshot. Such units run once and stay inactive by design, so their status module would be permanently 0.
  • -v, --verbose reports the diagnostics described in Diagnostics on standard error. It never changes the exit code, so it is safe to leave enabled while tuning a list.

docs.title: Combine and order the flags
docs.text:
• --default, --list and --help are actions: the first well-formed one in the command line wins and the later actions do not run. The value of --list and --exclude is checked even when the action does not win, so --default --list fails instead of running --default. Add --exclude, never a second action, to narrow a selection.
  • --usage, --exact-match, --skip-oneshot, -v and --exclude are not actions, so they can appear in any position and combine freely.
  • A --list or --exclude without a value, or with a value that starts with -, is rejected: the plugin prints the error and the help screen.
  • An unknown parameter is reported and followed by the help screen. The exit code stays 0 for every parameter problem, because the agent reads a non-zero exit as a plugin failure rather than as a configuration mistake. Unrecognized operating systems are the only non-zero exit. See Exit codes and streams.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Run the plugin manually on the endpoint with the same list you configured, and read the module XML it prints:

/usr/share/pandora_agent/plugins/autodiscover --default

<module>
    <name><![CDATA[Service sshd - Status]]></name>
    <type>generic_proc</type>
    <data><![CDATA[1]]></data>
</module>
  • One <module> block per matched service. A run that matches nothing prints nothing at all.
  • The exit code is 0 in every case except an unrecognized operating system. Do not use it to detect a bad list: use -v instead.
  • In Pandora FMS, the agent ingests the printed modules on its next run, so Service sshd - Status appears in the module list of the agent that ran the plugin.

docs.title: Understand the results
docs.text:
Every service of the active list that exists in the service manager produces one status module; --usage adds up to two more modules per running service.

Module name Type Data Unit Parent Generated when Service <name> - Status generic_proc 1 running, 0 stopped or inactive — — The service exists in the service manager and matches the active list Service <name> - CPU usage generic_data CPU usage of the service process % Service <name> - Status --usage, service running, process found Service <name> - Memory usage generic_data Memory usage of the service process % Service <name> - Status --usage, service running, process found
  • <name> is the service name without the platform suffix. On systemd, the unit sshd.service produces Service sshd - Status.
  • A 0 is not necessarily a problem. The status is 1 only while the service is running. A stopped service and an inactive unit produce 0, and the module stays in Pandora FMS until it is deleted. A service that is not installed produces no module, so a name of the list with no module of its own is simply absent from the endpoint.
  • The usage modules are conditional. They are emitted only for a running service whose process can be resolved and whose CPU or memory usage is greater than zero, so a first run may produce the status module alone.
  • How the status is read. On systemd the unit is running when its active state is active; the plugin lists every unit, including inactive ones. With SysV the service <name> status output is read for is running / is stopped. On Windows the Service Control Manager report is used.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
With -v (or --verbose) the plugin writes one line per finding on standard error, prefixed with autodiscover: warning:. The exit code is never changed.

/usr/share/pandora_agent/plugins/autodiscover --list "nope" -v

autodiscover: warning: entry "nope" matched no service
  • An entry of --list or --exclude that matched no service is reported. With --default, entries for services that are not installed on the endpoint are reported the same way, which is why the diagnostics are opt-in: a default run would otherwise report the services the endpoint does not have.
  • On Windows, list entries under three characters are reported as discarded.
  • A --skip-oneshot run whose unit types could not be read reports that the filter was ignored.

docs.title: Execution limits
docs.text:
• The units are listed, and their type is read with --skip-oneshot, with a 30-second internal limit per systemctl call; the per-service lookup of the process used by --usage has a 5-second limit, and a service call has a 10-second limit.
  • The module_timeout of the shipped block is 30 seconds. Raise it if the endpoint has a very large number of units, because the limit of the agent applies to the whole run and not only to one command.
  • --usage adds one process lookup per running service, so it is slower than a status-only run.
  • The plugin exits by itself when it finishes, and it handles SIGTERM by writing a message on standard error and exiting with code 0.

docs.title: Troubleshoot
docs.text:
• The plugin prints nothing. No service of the active list matched. Check the list with -v, and remember that --default is matched against the whole service name.
  • A service is not monitored. The name in the list does not match the unit or service name of the endpoint, or the service is not installed. Use the exact name, or a pattern that matches it, and confirm it with -v.
  • A status module is permanently 0. The service is stopped or inactive, or the unit is of type oneshot. Use --skip-oneshot to drop the last case. A service that is not installed produces no module at all, so a missing module is not a status of 0.
  • Services you did not ask for appear. A --list entry is a substring or a regular expression unless --exact-match is used, so httpd also selects httpd-init on a Linux systemd host, and Spool also selects Spooler on Windows. Add --exact-match, or narrow the pattern.
  • No usage module appears for a running service. The service process could not be resolved, or its CPU and memory usage were both zero.
  • An unexpected line appears on standard error while the modules are correct. A non-zero exit of systemctl is reported as a real failure, and the run then produces no modules. The messages under -v are informational and do not affect the result.
  • The agent reports a plugin timeout. Raise module_timeout, reduce the list, or drop --usage.

docs.title: Command line parameters
docs.text:
Name Value Required Default Description --default — One action is required — Monitors the built-in list of the platform, matched exactly --list <name1,name2,...> One action is required — Monitors the given list, matched as substrings or regular expressions unless --exact-match is set --exclude <name1,name2,...> No — Removes matching services from the active list, using the same matching mode as the active list. Repeatable; the values accumulate --exact-match — No Disabled Matches every --list entry against the whole service name, case-insensitive --skip-oneshot — No Disabled Linux with systemd only: ignores units whose type is oneshot --usage — No Disabled Adds a CPU usage and a memory usage module for every running service -v, --verbose — No Disabled Reports diagnostics on standard error; never changes the exit code --help — No — Prints the help screen, including the built-in list of the platform

An action (--default, --list, --help) is mandatory in practice: with no argument, and with no recognized action, the plugin prints the help screen and monitors nothing.

docs.title: Matching rules
docs.text:
• Each entry of a --list or --exclude value is a case-insensitive pattern.
  • With --exact-match, and always for --default, the pattern must match the whole service name (cron does not match cronie). Without it, the pattern is matched anywhere in the name (cron matches cronie and crond), and regular expressions such as php[0-9.]*-fpm are allowed.
  • A trailing .service is removed from an entry before matching, so httpd.service is accepted as the service httpd. The suffix is kept when the rest of the entry contains any of \ ^ $ * + ? ( ) [ ] { } |, so a pattern such as .*\.service is used as written. The dot itself is not a metacharacter here, so a real name such as dbus-org.freedesktop.NetworkManager.service keeps working.
  • On Windows, entries shorter than three characters are discarded.
  • On Linux without systemd, the entries of --list are used as literal names of /etc/init.d scripts, so regular expressions do not apply there.

docs.title: Built-in default service list
docs.text:
--default matches each entry against the whole service name, case-insensitive. The entries are patterns, so versioned or instance-suffixed names are covered. Entries that do not exist on the endpoint are ignored.

Linux

httpd, apache2, nginx, slapd, postfix, mysqld, mysql, mariadb, postgresql(-\d+)?, oracle,
oracle(-\w+)*, mongod, mongodb, redis, redis-server, elasticsearch, rabbitmq-server, ssh, sshd,
cron, crond, cronie, chronyd, chrony, ntpd, ntp, docker, containerd, php-fpm, php[\d.]*-fpm,
haproxy, keepalived, tomcat, tomcat\d*

Windows

MySQL(\d+)?, postgresql(-x64-\d+)?, pgsql, OracleService\w*, Oracle\w*TNSListener, MSSQLSERVER,
MSSQL\$\w+, SQLSERVERAGENT, IISADMIN, Apache2\.\d+, nginx, W3svc, NTDS, DNS,
MSExchangeADTopology, MSExchangeServiceHost, MSExchangeSA, MSExchangeTransport, MSExchangeIS,
Spooler, TermService, wuauserv, DHCP, TeamViewer, AnyDesk

docs.title: Exit codes and streams
docs.text: Stream Content Standard output The module XML, one <module> block per module. Also the help screen, which is printed when no action is given, on --help and after an unknown parameter Standard error The error of an unknown or incomplete parameter, the messages prefixed with autodiscover: warning: when -v is set, and real failures such as a systemctl call that could not be run Exit code Meaning 0 Normal run, help screen, warning, an unknown parameter, or an error inside the plugin 1 The operating system is not recognized

docs.title: Azure PostgreSQL monitoring plugin
docs.text: Article last updated: 2026-10-26.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
The Azure PostgreSQL monitoring plugin reads Azure Monitor metrics for one Azure Database for PostgreSQL resource and turns them into a Pandora FMS agent: 16 metrics covering CPU, memory, disk I/O, storage, connections, network traffic and replication delay. It is a server plugin: Pandora FMS executes it on a server on the module interval, or you run it manually from a terminal.

Each run authenticates with a Microsoft Entra service principal, asks Azure Monitor for the average of every metric over a time window and builds one agent data document. It works only with the resource identifier in its configuration file: it does not connect to PostgreSQL, so it needs no database user or password and works even when the database is not reachable from the Pandora FMS server.

A run delivers its result in one of three ways:

  • Agent data file (default): the plugin writes an agent data XML file into the Pandora FMS data directory and prints 1.
  • Tentacle: with --tentacle_address, the plugin writes the same file, sends it with tentacle_client and then prints 1.
  • Module XML on standard output: with --as_agent_plugin 1, the plugin prints one <module> block per value on standard output and writes no file.

The plugin keeps no state between runs: every value it publishes is the average Azure Monitor returns for the requested window at execution time.

docs.title: Compatibility and availability
docs.text:
Scope State Evidence Addon version 1.0 (pandorafms.azure_postgresql) Documented target The version this page describes. See Addon identity Pandora FMS NG 784 and later Supported The Marketplace states that all its integrations are compatible with Pandora FMS NG 784 and later versions. A catalogue-wide statement covering this addon, not a test record An Azure subscription containing the PostgreSQL resource to monitor Required The plugin reads the Azure Monitor metrics of the resource identified in its configuration file A Microsoft Entra service principal allowed to read that resource Required Authentication uses a tenant ID, an application ID and a client secret. Prerequisite, not a compatibility statement Outbound HTTPS access from the Pandora FMS server to the Azure Monitor endpoints of the public Azure cloud Required The plugin queries Azure Monitor directly and exposes no endpoint, authority or proxy setting A Pandora FMS data directory writable by the user that runs the plugin, for file and Tentacle delivery Required --data_dir, /var/spool/pandora/data_in/ by default Sovereign or custom Azure clouds Not validated No endpoint or authority setting exists, so a non-public cloud cannot be selected from the plugin Host operating system and distribution Not validated No operating system record exists for version 1.0 Azure Database for PostgreSQL server type and version Not validated The plugin requests a fixed list of 16 metric names. No matrix of server types or versions has been recorded Tentacle delivery Not validated --tentacle_address needs a reachable tentacle_client; no such run has been recorded

The Marketplace record limits the download to licensed users. It carries no maintenance or deprecation statement; see Addon identity.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. A Pandora FMS installation with the Plugin Server enabled, the console to register the plugin and create the module, and a writable data directory for the delivery mode you choose.
  2. An Azure subscription with the Azure Database for PostgreSQL resource to monitor.
  3. A Microsoft Entra service principal and its secret, with read access to that resource.
  4. The resource identifier of the PostgreSQL resource, in the long /subscriptions/.../resourceGroups/.../providers/... form.
  5. The addon files on the Pandora FMS server that will execute the plugin.

docs.title: Prepare Azure access
docs.text:
1. In Microsoft Entra ID, choose or create an application registration for the monitoring. From its overview, copy the Directory (tenant) ID and the Application (client) ID.
  2. Create a client secret for that application and copy its value, not its identifier: the value is shown only when the secret is created.
  3. Grant the application read access to the PostgreSQL resource, or to the Resource Group that contains it. Read-only access is enough, because the plugin only reads the resource and its Azure Monitor metrics.
  4. Open the PostgreSQL resource in the Azure portal, select JSON view in the overview and copy the value of its id field. That string is the resource identifier the plugin needs.

Keep the secret value out of tickets, chat and screenshots. The plugin stores it in a plain-text file (see Credential and resource file).

docs.title: Install the addon
docs.text:
Download the addon package from the Marketplace entry, which is limited to licensed users:

https://marketplace.pandorafms.com/entries/pandorafms.azure_postgresql

The package contains the executable pandora_azurepostgresql and a configuration file template pandora_azurepostgresql.conf. Copy the executable to the Pandora FMS server that will run it and make it executable. The recommended directory for server plugins is /usr/share/pandora_server/util/plugin/; any directory readable and executable by the user that runs plugin modules works.

Put the configuration file where that same user can read it, outside the web root, and restrict it to its owner, because it holds the client secret.

docs.title: Credential and resource file
docs.text:
The plugin reads all its connection data from the file passed with --conf. It is plain text with one key:value line per setting:

#credentials
tenant_id:<TENANT_ID>
client_id:<CLIENT_ID>
secret:<CLIENT_SECRET>
#id resources
serverpostgres_id:<POSTGRES_RESOURCE_ID>
Key Required Description tenant_id Yes Directory (tenant) ID of the Microsoft Entra application client_id Yes Application (client) ID secret Yes Client secret value. Stored in plain text: restrict the file to its owner serverpostgres_id Yes Azure resource identifier of the PostgreSQL resource whose metrics are read

The file format is rigid in four ways that matter when you edit it:

  • The separator is : and only the text after the first colon is read, so a value cannot contain a colon. Do not add spaces around the value; leading and trailing spaces are trimmed.
  • Any line that contains # anywhere is ignored. A # after a value silently discards that whole setting, so keep comments on their own lines.
  • Each key is recognised by its name appearing anywhere in the line. Do not add extra keys whose names contain tenant_id, client_id, secret or serverpostgres_id.
  • The four keys must be present. A file missing any of them stops the run with an error before any module is generated. The message does not always name the key, so check all four when a run fails at start-up.

docs.title: Register the server plugin
docs.text:
Register the executable in the console so Pandora FMS can execute it as a server plugin:

  1. Open Servers → Plugins and click Register plugin.
  2. Set a name and a description for the plugin.
  3. In Plugin command, enter the absolute path of the executable on the Pandora FMS server, for example /usr/share/pandora_server/util/plugin/pandora_azurepostgresql.
  4. In Plugin parameters, combine the plugin macros _field1_, _field2_, ... with the flags:
--conf _field1_ --agent_name _field2_ --prefix_module _field3_ --data_dir _field4_
  1. In Macro parameters, describe each field:
Field Description Example value _field1_ Absolute path to the credential and resource file on the Pandora FMS server /etc/pandora/plugins/azure-postgresql.conf _field2_ Agent that will hold the modules Azure_PostgreSQL_prod _field3_ Prefix added to every module name prod _field4_ Pandora FMS data directory, read by the Data Server /var/spool/pandora/data_in/

Do not add --as_agent_plugin 1 to the registered parameters. That flag makes the plugin print module XML instead of writing the agent data file, and the plugin module would then publish that XML as its value instead of 1.

Each registered plugin serves several PostgreSQL resources: register it once and give each plugin module its own credential file, agent name and prefix.

docs.title: Create the plugin module
docs.text:
1. Open the agent that will hold the modules and create a module of type Plugin.
  2. Select the registered plugin and fill its macros with the file, agent name, prefix and data directory of the target resource.
  3. Save the module.

Every execution publishes every metric the resource returns, so create one plugin module per PostgreSQL resource. Several modules pointing at the same resource repeat the same queries on every interval.

docs.title: Choose the delivery mode
docs.text:
• Agent data file (default): the plugin writes the document into --data_dir and prints 1. Use it when the plugin runs on a Pandora FMS server, including a remote server.
  • Tentacle: add --tentacle_address <PANDORA_FMS_SERVER> and, when it is not 41121, --tentacle_port <PORT>. The plugin sends the document with tentacle_client and prints 1.
  • Module XML on standard output: add --as_agent_plugin 1 to inspect the generated modules from a terminal without writing a file.

Tentacle delivery has two limits worth knowing before you rely on it:

  • The plugin passes only the address and the port to the Tentacle client. It has no Tentacle password option, so a Tentacle server that requires one rejects the transfer.
  • A rejected transfer prints Tentacle error on standard error but the plugin still prints 1, and the data file stays in --data_dir. Check the agent in the console, not the printed value.

The Tentacle address and port are passed to the Tentacle client unquoted. Use a host name or an IP address only, without shell metacharacters.

docs.title: Credentials and transport
docs.text:
• The client secret lives in the configuration file in plain text. Make the file readable only by the user that runs the plugin, for example chmod 600 and the same owner.
  • The secret is never passed on the command line: the plugin receives only the path to the file, so the secret does not appear in the shell history or in the process list.
  • The plugin exposes no option to skip TLS certificate verification and no proxy setting. Authentication and metric queries use the Azure endpoints and the default certificate trust store of the machine that runs the plugin. Keep the system CA bundle current.
  • Use an application dedicated to Pandora FMS and grant it read access only to the resources you monitor. Rotating its secret means editing one line of the configuration file.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Run the plugin manually on the Pandora FMS server, under the same user that executes plugin modules, to inspect the modules it generates:

./pandora_azurepostgresql --conf <PATH_TO_CONFIG> --as_agent_plugin 1

A successful run prints one <module> block per metric value. When the window returns more than one value for a metric, the output repeats that module name:

<module>
    <name><![CDATA[cpu_percent]]></name>
    <type>generic_data</type>
    <data><![CDATA[12.5]]></data>
    <description><![CDATA[2026-10-27 09:00:00+00:00 Average CPU percentage]]></description>
</module>
<module>
    <name><![CDATA[active_connections]]></name>
    <type>generic_data</type>
    <data><![CDATA[3]]></data>
    <description><![CDATA[2026-10-27 09:00:00+00:00 Active connections]]></description>
</module>

The values and the description text above are illustrative; the module names, the types and the document structure are the ones the plugin produces.

The same run without the flag uses the default mode:

./pandora_azurepostgresql --conf <PATH_TO_CONFIG> --agent_name <AGENT_NAME>

It writes an agent data file into --data_dir and prints 1. The plugin module of a registered plugin publishes that 1, so a module value of 1 means the run reached delivery, not that the data reached the console.

To confirm ingestion, open the agent named by --agent_name and check that it carries the metric modules with recent timestamps. Values only appear when Azure Monitor returned data for the window: a metric with no value is absent from that run.

docs.title: Understand the results
docs.text:
A successful run produces one agent and its modules:

Property Value Agent name --agent_name; Azure_Monitor_Postgresql by default Agent alias Same as the agent name Agent description Azure PostgreSQL Metrics Group --group; Azure by default. The group must exist in the console Agent address Empty Agent interval Empty in the agent definition; an agent that already exists keeps its own interval Module names Azure Monitor metric name, with <prefix>_ in front when --prefix_module is set Module type generic_data for the 16 metrics; generic_data_string for the custom module Module value The average Azure Monitor returns for one data point of the window Module description The data point timestamp followed by the description Azure Monitor gives the metric Units, thresholds, module interval None. Configure them in the console on the generated module

The 16 modules fall into five groups:

  • Resource usage. cpu_percent, memory_percent and io_consumption_percent report the processor, memory and disk I/O consumption of the server.
  • Storage. storage_percent, storage_used and storage_limit report the data storage in use, and backup_storage_used the backup storage in use.
  • Server log storage. serverlog_storage_percent, serverlog_storage_usage and serverlog_storage_limit report the server log storage.
  • Connections and network. active_connections and connections_failed count connections, and network_bytes_egress and network_bytes_ingress report network traffic.
  • Replication. pg_replica_log_delay_in_seconds and pg_replica_log_delay_in_bytes report the replication delay.

docs.title: One module entry per data point
docs.text:
The plugin emits one module entry for every data point that has a value in the window. When Azure Monitor returns more than one point for a metric, the document repeats that module name with a different value and a different timestamp in its description. The default window is one hour at a 60-minute interval; --timespan changes the window and the interval together.

Pandora FMS identifies a module by its name, so repeated names collapse into a single module and only one of those values is kept. Treat each module as "the latest average Azure Monitor returned", and read the time series in Azure Monitor when you need the evolution inside the window. A metric the resource reports as null produces no entry at all, so its module stays at its previous value.

docs.title: The custom metric module
docs.text:
With both --metric and --name_module, the plugin adds one generic_data_string module named --name_module, prefixed when --prefix_module is set. It contains one list entry per data point of that metric, with this fixed text:

The Availity at <data point timestamp> is <average>

Availity is the literal spelling the plugin writes. The metric name in --metric is passed to Azure Monitor as given: it must exist for the resource, otherwise the run stops before generating any module. When no data point has a value, the module is generated with an empty list.

The custom module is additional: the 16 standard metrics are still collected on the same run. --metric alone, or --name_module alone, adds nothing.

docs.title: Operate and troubleshoot
docs.text:
• Every run performs one Azure Monitor query per metric: sixteen by default, plus one for the custom module. The queries are sequential and none is retried, and a rejected query stops the run before the agent data file is written, so a run either publishes the whole set or none of it.
  • The window is --timespan hours with the interval derived from it: 1 hour at 60 minutes, 6 hours at 360, 12 hours at 720 and 24 hours at 1440. Any other value silently falls back to 1 hour. --granularity is accepted and has no effect: the interval always comes from --timespan.
  • Each run publishes averages of a whole window rather than the latest instantaneous value, so running the plugin more often than the interval does not add resolution. Set the module interval to the window you want to follow.
  • The plugin has no verbose or debug flag. The diagnostic channels are standard output, standard error and the exit status. A run that reaches delivery exits with status 0, an invalid command line exits with status 2, and a run that stops on an error exits with a non-zero status.
Signal Cause and check error: the following arguments are required: -c/--conf, exit status 2 The configuration file was not passed. The --conf flag is mandatory A usage summary naming an invalid value, exit status 2 A non-integer --timespan or --as_agent_plugin, or a flag left without a value An error before any module is generated, and no data file The configuration file lacks one of the four keys, or its credential or resource identifier cannot be read. Check the four keys and the # rule first An authentication or authorization error from Azure, no module Wrong tenant ID, application ID or secret, an expired secret, or an application without access to the resource. Test the credential outside Pandora FMS first An error about one metric and no module at all Azure Monitor rejected a metric name for that resource. Confirm that the resource exposes the 16 metric names listed in Generated modules ERROR - Could not write file: ..., please check directory permissions --data_dir does not exist or is not writable, or two runs started within the same second and the second one collided with the first file name. Retry, and check the directory permissions Tentacle error on standard error and 1 on standard output The Tentacle transfer failed: tentacle_client is missing or unreachable, the port is wrong, or the Tentacle server requires a password. The data file stays in --data_dir The plugin module value is module XML instead of 1 --as_agent_plugin 1 is in the registered parameters. Remove it 1 printed but no agent in the console The data file was written where the Data Server does not read it. Compare --data_dir with the server's incoming directory, and check that the plugin ran as a user with write permission on it The agent exists with fewer modules than expected Those metrics had no value in the window, or the resource does not report them. Remove null metrics from your expectations, not from the run A metric module shows an older value between runs The resource returned no value for the last runs, so the module kept its previous value. Confirm in Azure Monitor The agent lands in the wrong group The --group name is written as given and the group must exist in the console

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
./pandora_azurepostgresql --conf <PATH_TO_CONFIG> [options]
Name Required Default Description -c, --conf Yes — Path to the credential and resource file --timespan No 1 Window in hours: 1, 6, 12 or 24. Any other value is replaced by 1 --granularity No Derived from --timespan Accepted and ignored. The interval is always 60, 360, 720 or 1440 minutes, derived from --timespan --metric No Empty Azure Monitor metric name for the custom module. Only used together with --name_module --name_module No Empty Name of the custom module. Only used together with --metric --prefix_module No Empty Prefix joined to every module name with _ --agent_name No Azure_Monitor_Postgresql Name of the agent written in the agent data file -g, --group No Azure Group written in the agent definition --data_dir No /var/spool/pandora/data_in/ Directory where the agent data file is written --tentacle_address No Empty Tentacle server address. When set, the data file is sent with tentacle_client --tentacle_port No 41121 Tentacle server port --as_agent_plugin No 0 1 prints the module XML on standard output; any other integer value writes the agent data file and prints 1 -h, --help No — Print the help and exit

docs.title: Configuration file
docs.text:
tenant_id:<TENANT_ID>
client_id:<CLIENT_ID>
secret:<CLIENT_SECRET>
serverpostgres_id:<POSTGRES_RESOURCE_ID>
Key Required Description tenant_id Yes Directory (tenant) ID of the Microsoft Entra application client_id Yes Application (client) ID secret Yes Client secret value serverpostgres_id Yes Azure resource identifier of the PostgreSQL resource

key:value lines, no colon inside a value, and any line containing # is ignored as a whole. Keys are matched by name anywhere in the line.

docs.title: Generated modules
docs.text:
The plugin requests these 16 metric names on every run. The module name is the metric name, or <prefix>_<metric> when --prefix_module is set, and the value is the average Azure Monitor returns for one data point:

Metric What it reports cpu_percent Processor consumption of the server memory_percent Memory consumption of the server io_consumption_percent Disk I/O consumption of the server storage_percent Data storage used, as a percentage of the limit storage_used Data storage used storage_limit Data storage limit serverlog_storage_percent Server log storage used, as a percentage of the limit serverlog_storage_usage Server log storage used serverlog_storage_limit Server log storage limit active_connections Active connections connections_failed Failed connections backup_storage_used Backup storage used network_bytes_egress Network traffic sent network_bytes_ingress Network traffic received pg_replica_log_delay_in_seconds Replication delay in seconds pg_replica_log_delay_in_bytes Replication delay in bytes

The meaning of each value is the one Azure Monitor assigns to the metric name; the plugin forwards the average and adds no unit, so interpret the value with the metric name and configure the unit in the console.

With --metric <METRIC> --name_module <NAME> the run adds one generic_data_string module, named --name_module or <prefix>_<name_module>, whose list holds one entry per data point in the form The Availity at <timestamp> is <average>.
