docs.title: Journalctl plugin
docs.text: Article last updated: 2026-10-26.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
The Journalctl plugin forwards the systemd journal of a Linux host to Pandora FMS. On every run it asks journalctl for the entries written since the previous run, filters them with regular expressions and prints them as Pandora FMS log entries on standard output.

It is an agent plugin: the Pandora FMS agent runs it as one of its module_plugin lines, at every agent interval, and appends the entries it prints to its own data. The plugin creates no agent, opens no network connection and needs no credential: it only reads the journal of the machine where it runs.

Collection is incremental. The plugin keeps the time of its last successful run in a single file under /tmp and asks for the journal written after that moment, so each run delivers the new entries instead of the whole journal. A regular expression narrows what is delivered, either by keeping only the lines that match or by dropping the ones that match.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Scope State Evidence Addon pandorafms.journalctl, version 1.0 Documented target The version of the Marketplace package pandorafms.journalctl.1.0.zip. See Addon identity A Linux host with systemd and journalctl in the PATH Required journalctl is the only data source of the plugin: when the command is not available the run ends with an error and prints no entries An account allowed to read the journal Required The plugin reads the journal through journalctl with the permissions of the account that runs the agent; when the journal cannot be read the command fails and the run ends with an error A Pandora FMS agent installed on the monitored host Required The plugin is executed by the agent and its output is consumed as agent plugin output Pandora FMS NG 784 and later Supported The Marketplace states that all its integrations are compatible with Pandora FMS NG 784 and later versions. It is a general Marketplace statement, not a statement specific to this addon Individual Linux distributions and versions Not validated No distribution or version matrix is recorded for this addon

The plugin runs on the monitored host itself: it reports the journal of that host only, and it has no remote execution mode and no connection to another system.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. systemd, with the journalctl command available in the PATH of the account that runs the agent. The plugin has no fallback: without the command there is nothing to read.
  2. Journal read access for that account. The agent runs the plugin as its own user and the plugin does not elevate privileges. Grant that user the journal read access of your distribution — commonly through the systemd-journal group — or run the agent under an account that already has it. When the account cannot read the journal, journalctl fails and the run aborts.
  3. A writable /tmp. The plugin checks it at the start of every run and aborts when it cannot write there, because it keeps its collection position in /tmp/journalctl_logs.index.
  4. A Pandora FMS agent on the host. The agent is what turns the printed entries into log data in the console.
  5. A Marketplace account with a licence. The download of this addon is limited to licensed users.

docs.title: Install the plugin
docs.text:
Download the package from the Marketplace entry:

https://marketplace.pandorafms.com/entries/pandorafms.journalctl

The package distributes the grep_journalctl executable — that is the file name, not the addon identifier — and no configuration file. Copy it to the plugins directory of the agent and make it executable. On a Linux agent the plugins directory is /usr/share/pandora_agent/plugins, which is also reachable as /etc/pandora/plugins:

cp grep_journalctl /usr/share/pandora_agent/plugins/
chmod 755 /usr/share/pandora_agent/plugins/grep_journalctl

The agent adds its plugins directory to the PATH, so the bare executable name is enough in the module_plugin line. An absolute path also works and is the safer choice when more than one copy of the file exists.

Instead of copying the file by hand, the agent can distribute it to its hosts as a file collection; the destination is the same plugins directory.

docs.title: Add the plugin to the agent
docs.text:
The plugin is configured in the agent configuration file (pandora_agent.conf) as one module_plugin line. Without options it delivers every new journal line of the host:

module_plugin grep_journalctl

The line runs once per agent interval, so the coverage of each run is the time elapsed since the previous run. Restart or reload the agent after editing the file.

Narrow the delivery with an inclusion filter, and name the source that will group the entries in the console:

module_plugin grep_journalctl -in 'Failed password|authentication failure' -s AuthErrors

Or drop the lines you do not want and keep everything else:

module_plugin grep_journalctl -out 'session opened|session closed' -s SystemLog

A single module_plugin line per host is enough: see One collection position per host before adding a second one.

To bound the duration of the run, use the block form and add a module timeout. The block needs no module_name: the plugin prints its own entries and the agent appends them unchanged.

module_begin
module_plugin grep_journalctl -in 'error|critical' -s SystemErrors
module_timeout 120
module_end

The single-line form has no timeout, which means a run that reads a long backlog can last longer than the agent interval. module_timeout is expressed in seconds and applies to that line only.

When the agent reads its configuration from the console (remote configuration), the module_plugin line belongs to the agent configuration stored there, and a local edit of pandora_agent.conf is overwritten by the agent.

docs.title: Quote the patterns
docs.text:
The agent executes the module_plugin line through a shell, before the plugin sees it. A pattern that contains characters such as |, (, ), $, * or & must be quoted, or the shell interprets it and the plugin receives something else:

module_plugin grep_journalctl -in 'Failed password|authentication failure'

Use single quotes: they protect every character except a single quote of its own. Double quotes also work, but the shell still expands $ inside them, so a pattern such as end$ must be written with single quotes.

docs.title: Choose the source
docs.text:
-s / --source sets the source name that the console uses to group the entries of this line. The default is Journalctl, with a capital J. Always set a non-empty value: an empty -s '' is accepted and produces entries with an empty source, which makes them hard to find and to tell apart.

Changing the source does not reset the collection position. Entries delivered before the change stay under the previous source, and new entries appear under the new one, so a renamed source looks like a new journal in the console.

docs.title: Filter the lines
docs.text:
Both filters take a regular expression that is searched anywhere in the line. They are optional and only one of them can act:

  • -in / --regex_in keeps only the lines that match.
  • -out / --regex_out drops the lines that match.

When both are given, -in wins and -out is ignored without any warning. An empty value (-in '') counts as absent, so it does not filter anything.

Matching rules:

  • The expression is a search, not a full-line match: error matches any line that contains error.
  • Matching is case-sensitive unless the pattern turns it off with (?i): -in '(?i)error' matches ERROR and Error.
  • The whole journal line is matched, including the date, the host name and the unit prefix that journalctl writes in its default output format. A pattern anchored with ^ therefore sees the timestamp, not the message text: ^error matches almost nothing, while : error or (?i)error work as expected.
  • Each physical line is matched and delivered separately. An entry whose message spans several lines arrives as several entries, and a pattern cannot match across them.
  • A pattern that is not a valid regular expression aborts the run before the journal is read, with an error message and exit status 1.

The filter acts on the collected lines, after the collection position has advanced: a line that the filter drops is not delivered later and is never reconsidered. Changing the pattern does not replay the past.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Run the plugin by hand before wiring it into the agent. From the plugins directory:

./grep_journalctl

Each run executes once and exits. A successful run prints one <log_module> block per delivered line on standard output, and writes the collection position to /tmp/journalctl_logs.index:

<log_module>
    <source><![CDATA[Journalctl]]></source>
    <data>"Tm92IDExIDEyOjUzOjAyIGhvc3QwMSBzc2hkWzEzODJdOiBGYWlsZWQgcGFzc3dvcmQgZm9yIGludmFsaWQgdXNlciBhZG1pbiBmcm9tIDE5Mi4wLjIuMTA="</data>
    <encoding>base64</encoding>
</log_module>

<log_module>
    <source><![CDATA[Journalctl]]></source>
    <data>"Tm92IDExIDEyOjUzOjAzIGhvc3QwMSBzeXN0ZW1kWzFdOiBTdGFydGVkIFNlc3Npb24gNDIgb2YgdXNlciBtb25pdG9yaW5nLg=="</data>
    <encoding>base64</encoding>
</log_module>

The value of <data> is the journal line encoded in Base64, between double quotes. Decode it to confirm what was captured:

printf 'Tm92IDExIDEyOjUzOjAzIGhvc3QwMSBzeXN0ZW1kWzFdOiBTdGFydGVkIFNlc3Npb24gNDIgb2YgdXNlciBtb25pdG9yaW5nLg==' | base64 -d

Nov 11 12:53:03 host01 systemd[1]: Started Session 42 of user monitoring.

Run the same command again immediately. When no journal line was written in between, the run prints nothing on standard output, prints No new logs. on standard error and exits with status 0:

19:51:45 [INFO] No new logs.

The collection position that was written by the successful run can be read directly:

cat /tmp/journalctl_logs.index

2026-10-26 19:51:45

A manual run behaves exactly like an agent run, including the advance of that file. Use it to install, to test patterns and to diagnose, and take it into account when the agent is already running the same plugin on that host (see Everyday operation).

Once the module_plugin line is in place and the agent has run it, the entries appear in the console log viewer under the agent that runs the plugin and the source you configured:

docs.title: Log entries
docs.text:
Each delivered journal line becomes one log_module entry with three fields:

Field Content source The value of -s / --source, verbatim. The console groups the entries by this name. Default Journalctl data The journal line encoded in Base64, between double quotes encoding Always base64

Base64 is what keeps the generated XML valid: the journal can contain angle brackets, quotes and control characters, and the encoding carries them without breaking the document. The console decodes the value, so the log viewer shows the original line.

The plugin sends no module with a numeric value, no availability check and no alert template: log entries are its only output. Nothing appears in the monitoring views of the agent as a graph or as a status, so any alerting is configured in the console on top of the log data.

docs.title: What the agent does with the output
docs.text:
• The agent appends the plugin output to the data it sends to the server, so the <log_module> blocks reach Pandora FMS unchanged.
  • When the plugin exits with a status other than 0, the agent discards its entire output and records the error code in its own log. A run that fails after printing part of its entries delivers none of them.
  • The agent sends the standard error of a plugin to /dev/null. Every diagnostic of this plugin — the regex error, the journalctl failure, the missing /tmp permission, the No new logs. notice and the -v line — is therefore invisible in a scheduled run. Run the command by hand to read it.

docs.title: Coverage and the collection position
docs.text:
The plugin stores one timestamp, in the format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, in /tmp/journalctl_logs.index. Each run asks journalctl for the entries since that moment:

journalctl --since "<stored timestamp>" --no-pager

The window of a run therefore starts where the previous successful run ended and finishes when the current run writes its own timestamp. That position is written at the very end of the run and only when the run completes. Three consequences follow, and they are worth knowing before you rely on the log for auditing:

  • The run covers everything since the last completed run. This includes entries written while the plugin was stopped, so a host whose agent was down for a day delivers a day of journal in the first run after it starts. There is no line limit: the whole window is read into memory and printed one entry per line.
  • A run that fails does not advance the position. Nothing is lost, but the next successful run repeats the same window, so entries can be delivered twice: after a failed journalctl, after an invalid regular expression, and after a run interrupted with Ctrl+C or killed before it finishes.
  • A small part of the window is never delivered. The position is the time at the end of the run, while the journal was read earlier in the same run. Entries written between the read and the write of the timestamp are older than the stored position when the next run starts, so they are skipped. The gap is short, but it exists.

Two smaller effects of the same design:

  • The timestamp has a resolution of one second and the query includes the entries written in that exact second, so a line written in the same second in which the previous run ended can be delivered twice.
  • The timestamp carries no time zone and journalctl reads it in the local time of the host. If the host changes its time zone or crosses a daylight-saving transition, the window between two runs shifts accordingly.

docs.title: One collection position per host
docs.text:
The file name is fixed: every execution of the plugin on the same host uses /tmp/journalctl_logs.index, whatever source, filter or account it uses. There is no per-module or per-source state.

  • Two module_plugin lines on the same host share the position. The second line finds an almost empty window, because the first one already consumed it, and each of them receives an arbitrary part of the journal. Do not run two lines: keep one and use -in to select what you need.
  • A manual run and the scheduled run share it too, so a manual run consumes the window that the agent would have delivered.

The position file lives in a shared directory

/tmp is world-writable and the file name is fixed, so any local account can create that file first, replace it, or turn it into a symbolic link. The plugin writes its timestamp with the privileges of the agent account, so a symbolic link placed there makes the run overwrite another file that this account can write. Run the agent with an unprivileged account where your installation allows it, and do not treat the content of the file as a tamper-proof record.

docs.title: First run
docs.text:
When /tmp/journalctl_logs.index does not exist, or its content cannot be read or is not a valid timestamp, the run collects the last five minutes of the journal. This is also what happens after a reboot that clears /tmp: journal entries of the five minutes before the reboot can be delivered a second time, because the journal may survive the reboot while the position does not.

To force that five-minute window again, delete the file:

rm -f /tmp/journalctl_logs.index

The next run starts from five minutes before it, whatever happened in between.

docs.title: Everyday operation
docs.text:
• One line per host. The single collection position makes a second line useless (see One collection position per host).
  • The interval sets the coverage. The agent runs the line at the agent interval, and each run covers what happened since the previous one. A shorter interval delivers more often and in smaller batches; it does not change which entries are delivered.
  • Bound long runs. After a long stop, the first run reads the whole window. Set module_timeout in a block so that a large backlog cannot delay the agent beyond the interval, and run the plugin by hand first to drain it.
  • Manual runs consume data. A manual run prints the entries to your terminal and advances the position, so the agent does not deliver them afterwards. Use the manual run for installation, for trying a pattern and for diagnosis, and expect the next agent run to be empty.
  • -v only reports the position write. The verbose mode raises the diagnostic level, but the only message it adds is the line that records the new collection position, for example 19:51:53 [DEBUG] Saved execution time: 2026-10-26 19:51:53 -> /tmp/journalctl_logs.index. It does not report the applied filters, the number of lines read or the number of entries delivered.
  • Keep the patterns stable. A filter change applies from the next run on; the lines already dropped are gone, and a line the new pattern would have kept is not recovered.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Check No entries in the console, and the manual run prints nothing The window is empty: another run (the agent, or your own earlier manual run) has already consumed it, or the filter drops everything Run the plugin by hand with the same options, right after writing a matching test line with logger 'test journalctl' No new logs. at every run The position advances but no line passes the filter, or a second execution consumes the window first Check the filters against real lines with journalctl --since '10 minutes ago' --no-pager; keep one module_plugin line Entries appear under the wrong source -s is missing (default Journalctl), or it was changed and the old entries stayed under their old source Set -s explicitly, and look for the previous source in the log viewer A pattern that works elsewhere matches nothing The line carries journalctl's date and host prefix, or the case does not match Remove the ^ anchor, or add (?i) Invalid regex: ... and no entries The pattern is not a valid regular expression Fix the pattern; the run stops before reading the journal, so nothing is lost Error: 'journalctl' command not found... journalctl is not installed or not in the PATH of the agent Install systemd, or make sure the PATH of the agent includes the directory that contains journalctl Error executing journalctl: ... followed by the command error journalctl failed: the account cannot read the journal, or the journal is unreadable Run journalctl --since '5 minutes ago' --no-pager as the agent user No write permissions for /tmp /tmp is not writable by the account that runs the plugin Fix the permissions or the mount options of /tmp The run ends with status 2 and a usage message An unknown option, or an option without a value Compare the line with Command-line parameters Entries disappear after a run that also failed The exit status was not 0, so the agent discarded the whole output Look for the error in a manual run: the agent already turned the standard error into /dev/null Some entries are missing between two runs They were written while the run was in progress, or the filter dropped them This is expected: the window ends at the moment the position is written The same entries arrive twice The previous run did not complete, the position was deleted, /tmp was cleared, or the two runs ended in the same second Accept it, or use the entry timestamp in the console to identify the duplicate

docs.title: Command-line parameters
docs.text:
Name Required Default Description -in <regex>, --regex_in <regex> No None (every line) Delivers only the journal lines that match the expression. An empty value counts as absent. Takes precedence over -out -out <regex>, --regex_out <regex> No None (nothing excluded) Drops the journal lines that match the expression. Ignored when -in is set -s <name>, --source <name> No Journalctl Value of the source field of every entry. An empty value produces entries with an empty source -v, --verbose No Off Raises the diagnostic level. The only additional message is the one that records the new collection position -h, --help No — Prints the usage summary and exits with status 0

Values are given as -in <value> or --regex_in <value>; the forms -in=<value> and --regex_in=<value> are also accepted. Options can be given in any order.

The agent adds two directives of its own around the same line, in the block form: module_timeout <seconds> to bound the run and module_end to close the block. They belong to the agent configuration, not to the plugin.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Situation Standard output Standard error Exit status At least one line survives the filters One <log_module> block per line, each followed by a blank line Nothing 0 The journal holds no entry in the window Nothing HH:MM:SS [INFO] No new logs. 0 Every collected line is filtered out Nothing Nothing 0 The regular expression is invalid Nothing HH:MM:SS [ERROR] Invalid regex: <reason> 1 journalctl is not available Nothing HH:MM:SS [ERROR] Error: 'journalctl' command not found... 1 journalctl fails Nothing HH:MM:SS [ERROR] Error executing journalctl: ... and the command error 1 /tmp is not writable Nothing HH:MM:SS [ERROR] No write permissions for /tmp 1 A processing error while building the entries The entries printed so far HH:MM:SS [ERROR] Error processing logs: <reason> 1 Interrupted with Ctrl+C during the processing The entries printed so far HH:MM:SS [INFO] Execution interrupted. 0 -h, --help Usage summary Nothing 0 Unknown option or missing value Nothing Usage message and the error 2

The HH:MM:SS prefix is the local time of the message. Every diagnostic of the plugin goes to standard error, and standard output carries only the entry XML.

docs.title: Collection position
docs.text: Property Value Path /tmp/journalctl_logs.index Content A single line with the timestamp of the end of the last successful run, in the format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, local time without a time zone Written when At the end of a run that completes, including a run whose lines were all filtered out Not written when journalctl fails, the regular expression is invalid, /tmp is not writable, or the run is interrupted Read when At the start of every run. A missing file, or a content that is not a valid timestamp, starts the window five minutes before the run Scope One file per host, shared by every execution of the plugin on that host, whatever source, filter or account

docs.title: Kafka monitoring plugin
docs.text: Article last updated: 2026-10-26.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
The Kafka monitoring plugin collects the performance metrics of a Kafka client and publishes them as Pandora FMS modules. Each run creates a producer and a consumer against one Kafka endpoint, takes a snapshot of the metrics both clients report, and writes the result into a Pandora FMS agent.

The plugin is a server plugin: the Pandora FMS Plugin Server executes it, and each run delivers the generated agent XML to Pandora FMS through Tentacle or into a local data directory. Nothing is installed on the Kafka broker.

What the plugin measures has three consequences worth stating before you configure it:

  • It does not read Kafka broker JMX metrics. The modules describe the producer and consumer clients that the plugin creates, not the producers and consumers of your applications, and not the broker's own MBeans.
  • It does not send or consume records. The plugin creates both clients, optionally subscribes the consumer to topics, reads the metric snapshot and closes them. It does not poll the consumer and commits no offsets.
  • It creates one agent per --bootstrap_servers entry. Two successfully processed endpoints produce two agents, even when both point to the same cluster.

The plugin prints 1 when it processed every endpoint without an exception and 0 when any endpoint raised one. That printed value is what a Pandora FMS plugin module receives. A broker that cannot be reached makes the run print 0; the value does not prove that the generated agent was delivered, so verify delivery separately (see Verify).

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Scope State Evidence Addon pandorafms.apache_kafka, version 1.1 Documented target The version this page describes. See Addon identity Pandora FMS NG 784 and later Supported The Marketplace states that all integrations are compatible with Pandora FMS NG 784 and later versions. This is a catalogue-wide statement covering the addon, not a test record for it A Kafka listener reachable from the Pandora FMS server over TCP Required The plugin connects to every endpoint listed in --bootstrap_servers A listener that accepts unauthenticated PLAINTEXT connections Required The addon exposes no options for SASL authentication or TLS, so it can only use the Kafka client's default connection settings Rocky Linux Known compatible The legacy guide for this addon records Rocky Linux as the system where it was tested. Not re-validated for version 1.1 Other Linux distributions Not validated No distribution range or version matrix has been recorded for this addon Kafka broker versions Not validated No broker version matrix has been recorded for this addon tentacle_client in PATH Required when --transfer_mode is not local Tentacle delivery runs that command Write access to /tmp Required The plugin stages the generated XML in /tmp before delivery Write access to /var/spool/pandora/data_in/ Required when --transfer_mode local is used The XML document is moved into that directory

No compatibility statement establishes a Kafka version range, a broker distribution or a Linux distribution other than the Rocky Linux record above. Keep each claim at the scope its source proves.

docs.title: Kafka requirements
docs.text:
1. A reachable Kafka listener. Use the listener address and port in --bootstrap_servers, for example <TARGET_HOST>:9092. Include the port explicitly in every endpoint; Kafka's default client port is 9092.
  2. A listener that accepts the client's default connection. The addon has no security_protocol, SASL or TLS options. A cluster whose listeners require SASL authentication, TLS client certificates or another authenticated protocol cannot be monitored with this version.
  3. No Kafka account or JMX access. The plugin authenticates with nothing, so it needs no Kafka user, no JMX port and no RMI credentials. If anonymous access to the listener is disabled, the connection fails and the run reports it only as a broker processing error.

The plugin does not read or write topic data, so it needs no topic ACL for the applications you monitor. Restrict the listener to the Pandora FMS server network instead of opening it broadly.

docs.title: Pandora FMS requirements
docs.text:
1. Pandora FMS with the Plugin Server enabled on the server that will run the plugin.
  2. A Tentacle server reachable at --tentacle_ip and --tentacle_port when the default Tentacle delivery is used, plus the tentacle_client command in PATH.
  3. A writable data directory when --transfer_mode local is used. The plugin moves the XML into /var/spool/pandora/data_in/; the option does not let you choose another directory.
  4. Write access to /tmp for the user that runs the Plugin Server. The generated XML is staged there before delivery.

docs.title: Install the plugin
docs.text:
Download the addon from its Marketplace entry, whose download is limited to licensed users:

https://marketplace.pandorafms.com/entries/pandorafms.apache_kafka

Copy the pandora_kafka executable to the Pandora FMS server and give it execute permission. The recommended directory for server plugins is:

/usr/share/pandora_server/util/plugin/

sudo chmod 755 /usr/share/pandora_server/util/plugin/pandora_kafka

Nothing is installed on the Kafka broker, and the Kafka server does not need JMX enabled.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
The plugin has no configuration file. It takes all its settings from the command line, starting from built-in defaults:

built-in defaults < command-line options

Every option is documented in Command-line parameters. This section explains the decisions that change what the plugin measures and where the result goes.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
--bootstrap_servers is mandatory and accepts a comma-separated list of Kafka endpoints in host:port form:

--bootstrap_servers <KAFKA_HOST_1>:9092,<KAFKA_HOST_2>:9092

Each non-empty item is processed independently and produces one agent. Empty items between commas are ignored. The plugin does not create one agent per cluster broker: it creates one producer and one consumer per item and names the agent after that item.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
The consumer can subscribe to a list of topics, a regular expression, or nothing:

  • --topics orders,payments subscribes to the listed topics.
  • --topic_regex '^prod-.*' subscribes to the topics that match the pattern.
  • When both are given, --topic_regex takes precedence and --topics is ignored.
  • When neither is given, the consumer is created without a subscription.

Subscription does not make the plugin read messages. It never polls the consumer, so no records are consumed and no offsets are committed. The consumer uses the fixed group identifier monitoring-client with automatic commit disabled.

An invalid regular expression is not rejected before the run starts: the error is printed only with --verbose, and the subscription then raises during that endpoint's processing, which makes the run print 0. Test the pattern with --verbose before registering it.

docs.title: Agent and module prefixes
docs.text:
--agent_prefix is prepended to both the name and the alias of every generated agent, and --module_prefix is prepended to every generated module name. Both default to an empty string.

--agent_prefix KAFKA_ --module_prefix METRIC_

With the broker kafka1:9092, the agent is named KAFKA_kafka1:9092, and the module producer-metrics.request-rate becomes METRIC_producer-metrics.request-rate.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
The default is Tentacle delivery. --transfer_mode accepts one meaningful value:

Value Behavior tentacle (default) Sends the XML document with tentacle_client to --tentacle_ip:--tentacle_port local Moves the XML document into /var/spool/pandora/data_in/ Any other value, including a misspelling Also uses Tentacle; the plugin only treats the exact value local as local delivery

--tentacle_ip defaults to 127.0.0.1 and --tentacle_port to 41121. They are only used by Tentacle delivery. Local delivery has no configurable folder: if the Pandora FMS server does not use /var/spool/pandora/data_in/, use Tentacle instead.

Tentacle failures are printed on standard error, but they do not change the 1 or 0 the plugin prints. See Output and exit status.

docs.title: Register the plugin in the console
docs.text:
1. Open Servers → Plugins and click Register Plugin.
  2. Set a name, the plugin type Standard, an optional maximum timeout and a description.
  3. In Plugin command, enter the full path to the executable on the Pandora FMS server: /usr/share/pandora_server/util/plugin/pandora_kafka.
  4. In Plugin parameters, combine the mandatory endpoint with the options you need, using the plugin macros _field1_, _field2_, ... as placeholders:
--bootstrap_servers _field1_ --agent_prefix _field2_ --module_prefix _field3_ --transfer_mode tentacle --tentacle_ip 127.0.0.1 --tentacle_port 41121
  1. In Macro parameters, describe each field. The example uses these values:
Field Description Example value _field1_ Kafka endpoint, including the port; several endpoints separated by commas <KAFKA_HOST>:9092 _field2_ Prefix for the generated agent names and aliases KAFKA_ _field3_ Prefix for the generated module names METRIC_

Add --topics _field4_ or --topic_regex _field4_ only when you want a subscription. Every flag that remains in the parameter string must receive a value: a blank macro leaves the flag without an argument, and the plugin exits with an argument-parsing error instead of running. Remove the flag rather than leaving its field empty.

After the server plugin is created, open an agent, create a plugin module and select the registered plugin. That module receives the printed 1 or 0. The Kafka metrics do not go into that module: they arrive in the separate agents the plugin creates.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• The addon has no user, password or token options, and no SASL or TLS settings. It connects with the Kafka client's default unauthenticated PLAINTEXT configuration.
  • Because there is no transport encryption, metrics and connection metadata travel in clear text between the Pandora FMS server and the Kafka listener. Restrict the listener to a trusted network, or do not use this addon where authentication or encryption is mandatory.
  • The plugin stores no credentials, so there is no secret to protect in a configuration file. Its command line only carries broker addresses, prefixes and delivery settings.
  • --verbose prints broker error details on standard output. Those messages can include broker addresses and exception text, so review them before sharing a manual run.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Run the plugin manually from a terminal on the Pandora FMS server:

./pandora_kafka \
  --bootstrap_servers <TARGET_HOST>:9092 \
  --topics <TOPIC> \
  --agent_prefix KAFKA_ \
  --transfer_mode tentacle \
  --tentacle_ip <PANDORA_FMS_SERVER> \
  --tentacle_port 41121 \
  --verbose

A successful run ends with 1 on standard output. With Tentacle delivery, the agent KAFKA_<TARGET_HOST>:9092 and its modules appear in Pandora FMS after the next data processing cycle. With local delivery, check that a .data file has been moved into /var/spool/pandora/data_in/ and that the agent appears after the data server processes it.

The printed value alone is not enough to verify the integration:

  • 1 means the plugin created the producer and the consumer for every endpoint and collected their metrics without an exception. Client creation resolves the broker version over the network, so a broker that rejects or does not answer the connection produces 0 instead.
  • 1 does not prove delivery: a Tentacle failure is printed on standard error but still leaves 1 on standard output.

Verify the data, not only the exit line:

  1. Confirm the generated agent exists and its name follows the prefix rule.
  2. Open its modules and check that connection and request metrics report activity.
  3. If every value is zero, check connectivity before assuming the plugin delivered correctly.

Use ./pandora_kafka -h to print the usage summary, the plugin version and the execution example.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
The plugin creates one agent per successfully processed non-empty --bootstrap_servers item. Name and alias use the same value:

<agent_prefix><host:port>

For example, with --agent_prefix KAFKA_ and the endpoint kafka1:9092, the agent is KAFKA_kafka1:9092. Every generated agent has an interval of 300 seconds, the description Created by plugin and no agent group assigned.

Running the plugin twice with the same endpoint updates the same agent name. Running it with two endpoints that belong to the same cluster creates two agents with duplicated module sets.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
The plugin iterates over every metric group and metric name reported by the producer and the consumer. The module name is:

<module_prefix><metric_group>.<metric_name>

All modules are created as generic_data, without a unit and without a description. Floating-point values that are NaN, positive infinity or negative infinity are written as 0.0.

The exact catalogue depends on the Kafka client state and the Kafka version. The stable groups and representative modules are:

Source Metric group Representative modules without prefix Producer and consumer kafka-metrics-count kafka-metrics-count.count Producer producer-metrics producer-metrics.connection-count, producer-metrics.request-rate, producer-metrics.request-latency-avg, producer-metrics.outgoing-byte-rate Producer producer-node-metrics.node-<node> producer-node-metrics.node-<node>.outgoing-byte-rate, producer-node-metrics.node-<node>.request-rate, producer-node-metrics.node-<node>.response-rate Consumer consumer-metrics consumer-metrics.connection-count, consumer-metrics.request-rate, consumer-metrics.incoming-byte-rate, consumer-metrics.request-latency-avg Consumer consumer-node-metrics.node-<node> consumer-node-metrics.node-<node>.incoming-byte-rate, consumer-node-metrics.node-<node>.request-rate, consumer-node-metrics.node-<node>.response-rate Consumer consumer-fetch-manager-metrics consumer-fetch-manager-metrics.fetch-size-avg, consumer-fetch-manager-metrics.bytes-consumed-rate, consumer-fetch-manager-metrics.records-consumed-rate, consumer-fetch-manager-metrics.records-lag-max Consumer consumer-coordinator-metrics consumer-coordinator-metrics.commit-rate, consumer-coordinator-metrics.assigned-partitions

In the node groups, <node> is the numeric Kafka node identifier, for example node-1. The group name already contains it, so a full module name looks like producer-node-metrics.node-1.outgoing-byte-rate. Node groups appear only for the nodes the probe client actually contacts; the set depends on the cluster metadata returned to that client.

Both clients register their own kafka-metrics-count group, so the generated agent XML contains kafka-metrics-count.count twice: once with the producer's count and once with the consumer's count. This is expected behavior, not a duplicated agent.

docs.title: What the values represent
docs.text:
Each run creates new clients and reads their metrics immediately. The values are therefore a snapshot of a freshly created probe, not a continuous sample of your application:

  • Connection counters, request counters and request latency describe the plugin's own client connections.
  • Record and commit rates describe traffic that the probe client does not generate: the plugin sends no records, polls no records and commits no offsets, so those rates normally remain at their initial values. Byte and request rates reflect only the probe's own connection and metadata traffic, not your application's throughput.
  • Averages that need samples from the client's lifetime can be 0.0 because the plugin converts their initial NaN to zero.
  • Consumer group metrics do not reflect your application's consumer groups. The consumer uses the fixed group identifier monitoring-client, with automatic commit disabled, and never joins a group during the run.

Use the connection and request metrics to observe whether the Kafka listener is reachable and responsive from the Pandora FMS server. Do not use this addon as a substitute for Kafka broker JMX monitoring or for instrumenting application producers and consumers.

docs.title: Operate and troubleshoot
docs.text:
The plugin keeps no state between executions. Every run creates its clients, collects one snapshot, delivers one agent document and exits, so it can be run manually at any time without affecting offsets or topic data.

Schedule the registered plugin module at the interval you want. The generated agents keep their fixed 300-second interval, but their values are refreshed only when the plugin module runs; align the module interval with the desired data cadence. Use --verbose for manual diagnosis, but do not leave it in the registered parameter string: its diagnostic lines are written to standard output and become part of the value the plugin module receives.

docs.title: Output and exit status
docs.text: Result Meaning Standard output 1 Every endpoint was processed without an exception: its clients were created and their metrics collected. Delivery is not guaranteed Standard output 0 At least one endpoint raised an exception, for example because the broker was unreachable or rejected the connection. Run again with --verbose to see the detail No standard output without --verbose The bootstrap list contained no non-empty item. The process exits with status 0 Argument-parsing error on standard error A required option is missing or a flag has no value, for example a blank macro field. The process exits with status 2 Process exit status 0 with 1 or 0 on standard output Normal run. The printed number is the module value, not the process status

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text:
• The run prints 1 but no agent appears. The broker processing succeeded but delivery failed. Check that tentacle_client exists in PATH and can reach --tentacle_ip:--tentacle_port. Run manually with --verbose and read standard error; Tentacle errors do not alter the printed 1. For local delivery, check that /var/spool/pandora/data_in/ exists and is writable.
  • The run prints 0. At least one endpoint failed. Run with --verbose and read the Error with broker ... line. The usual causes are a wrong address or port, a listener that requires authentication or TLS, an invalid --topic_regex, or a malformed endpoint.
  • The run prints nothing without --verbose. --bootstrap_servers was accepted but contained no non-empty item, for example a comma or spaces only. The process exits 0 without an agent or a value. Correct the endpoint list.
  • The plugin exits before connecting. An option is missing its value. This is the usual result of leaving a _fieldN_ macro empty for a flag that you kept in the parameter string. Remove the unused flag or fill the field.
  • The agent exists but every value is zero. The probe connected, but it did not exchange further data with the cluster. Check the listener address and port, and whether the listener accepts unauthenticated PLAINTEXT connections. Remember that record and commit rates are expected to stay at their initial values because the probe sends and consumes no records, and byte and request rates reflect only the probe's own traffic.
  • The cluster requires SASL or TLS. This version cannot connect to it. The addon has no option to configure authentication or encryption; use a Kafka monitoring path that supports those settings.
  • --transfer_mode local does not deliver. The plugin always moves the XML into /var/spool/pandora/data_in/. If the Pandora FMS server uses another data directory, use Tentacle delivery instead.
  • A misspelled transfer mode still tries Tentacle. Only the exact value local selects local delivery; every other value falls back to Tentacle.
  • Values look stale. Every run returns the snapshot taken at that moment. Check the plugin module interval and the broker state rather than expecting a continuous series.

docs.title: Command-line parameters
docs.text:
./pandora_kafka --bootstrap_servers <host:port> [--topics <topic1,topic2>] [--topic_regex <regex>] [--agent_prefix <prefix>] [--module_prefix <prefix>] [--transfer_mode <mode>] [--tentacle_ip <ip>] [--tentacle_port <port>] [--verbose]
Name Required Default Description -h, --help No — Prints the usage summary, the plugin version and the execution example, then exits --bootstrap_servers Yes — Comma-separated Kafka endpoints in host:port form. Empty items are ignored. Each remaining item produces one agent --topics No Empty Comma-separated topics for the consumer subscription. Ignored when --topic_regex is set --topic_regex No Empty Regular expression for the consumer subscription. Takes precedence over --topics. An invalid pattern fails during the run --agent_prefix No Empty Prefix added to the name and alias of every generated agent --module_prefix No Empty Prefix added to every generated module name --transfer_mode No tentacle local moves the XML into /var/spool/pandora/data_in/. Any other value, including the default, uses Tentacle --tentacle_ip No 127.0.0.1 Tentacle server address for Tentacle delivery --tentacle_port No 41121 Tentacle server port for Tentacle delivery --verbose No Disabled Prints broker error and diagnostic messages on standard output

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text: Setting Value Default delivery Tentacle Tentacle client command tentacle_client, resolved through PATH Tentacle address and port --tentacle_ip and --tentacle_port Local delivery selector --transfer_mode local (exact value) Local destination /var/spool/pandora/data_in/ Configurable local destination No XML staging directory /tmp Runtime dependency on the broker None; nothing is installed on the Kafka broker

docs.title: Generated agents
docs.text: Attribute Value Cardinality One agent per successfully processed non-empty --bootstrap_servers item Name <agent_prefix><host:port> Alias Same as the name Description Created by plugin Interval 300 seconds Group Not set Data source Producer and consumer metrics of the clients created in that run

docs.title: Consumer behaviour
docs.text: Behavior Value Consumer group identifier monitoring-client Automatic offset commit Disabled Records consumed None; the plugin never polls the consumer Offsets committed None Subscription Optional, through --topics or --topic_regex Effect on topic data None

docs.title: Metric groups
docs.text:
The plugin prefixes every module name with <module_prefix>. The metric part is <metric_group>.<metric_name>, where <node> is the numeric Kafka node identifier.

Source Metric group Example metric names Producer and consumer kafka-metrics-count count Producer producer-metrics connection-count, request-rate, request-latency-avg, outgoing-byte-rate, incoming-byte-rate Producer producer-node-metrics.node-<node> outgoing-byte-rate, incoming-byte-rate, request-rate, response-rate, request-latency-avg Consumer consumer-metrics connection-count, request-rate, request-latency-avg, incoming-byte-rate, outgoing-byte-rate Consumer consumer-node-metrics.node-<node> incoming-byte-rate, outgoing-byte-rate, request-rate, response-rate, request-latency-avg Consumer consumer-fetch-manager-metrics fetch-size-avg, fetch-size-max, bytes-consumed-rate, records-consumed-rate, records-lag-max Consumer consumer-coordinator-metrics commit-latency-avg, commit-latency-max, commit-rate, assigned-partitions

This list is a functional catalogue, not a fixed contract: the exact metric set depends on the Kafka client version and on the state of the clients at execution time. All generated modules use generic_data, with no unit and no description.

The metric definitions published by Kafka for its clients help interpret the values:

  • Consumer monitoring
  • Producer monitoring
